answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1880–1968 · American author, lecturer & disability rights advocate
answer.sourceLine: Both sentences are Helen Keller’s own words, printed on page 2 of her 1929 consolation book We Bereaved (New York: Leslie Fulenwider, Inc.) — confirmed in the scanned full text. One caveat worth knowing: in the original they are not adjacent. A sentence about a sunset, a moonlit mountain and the ocean stands between them, so the popular two-sentence quote is a faithful condensation rather than a continuous passage.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Verbatim — but one sentence is elided between the two

source.excerpt: What we have once enjoyed we can never lose. A sunset, a mountain bathed in moonlight, the ocean in calm and in storm — we see these, love their beauty, hold the vision to our hearts. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us. Our beloved ones are no more lost to us when they die than if they were still laughing and loving and working and playing at our side. Truly, life is overlord of Death and Love can never lose its own.
trail: 1929 — Helen Keller, We Bereaved (New York: Leslie Fulenwider, Inc.), page 2. Both sentences appear here, separated by one sentence about a sunset, a moonlit mountain and the ocean. Read them in the scanned full text ↗.
1957 — Quote Investigator reports ↗ that Keller’s The Open Door (Doubleday, 1957), page 131, reprinted the passage, widening its reach far beyond the slim 1929 booklet.
1990 — The rewritten, fused version appears credited to Keller in Sherokee Ilse’s Empty Arms (Wintergreen Press, 1990), page 24, per Quote Investigator’s citation trail ↗.
1996 — The New Beacon Book of Quotations by Women, compiled by Rosalie Maggio (Beacon Press), page 411, cited We Bereaved but condensed the passage — one of the steps QI documents ↗.
source.excerptNote: The familiar quote is the first and third sentences of this paragraph. Every word of it is Keller’s; what the popular version removes is the sunset sentence in between.

source.rightsNote: We Bereaved was first published in New York by Leslie Fulenwider, Inc. in 1929, with a copyright notice reading “Copyright, 1929, by Leslie Fulenwider, Inc.” First publication before 1931 puts the work in the public domain in the United States, which is why the complete book can be read freely at the Internet Archive ↗ and is hosted as a public-domain scan on Wikimedia Commons ↗. Note that the 1957 reprint in The Open Door is a separate, later publication; the wording quoted here is sourced to the 1929 original.

author.name: Helen Keller
author.heading: Who was Helen Keller?
author.metaLine: 1880–1968 · American author, lecturer & disability rights advocate
author.bio: Helen Adams Keller lost her sight and hearing in early childhood and, taught by Anne Sullivan, went on to become the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree, graduating from Radcliffe College in 1904. She spent the rest of her life as an author, lecturer and political activist, campaigning for disability rights, women’s suffrage, labour rights and peace. We Bereaved, a slim 39-page book of consolation published in 1929, is the home of one of her most-quoted and most-mangled sentences.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: This is the rare famous-name quote that survives inspection — the words really are Keller’s. What circulates most widely, however, is not this wording. It is a fused, rewritten sentence that no Keller book contains.

items.who: “What we have once enjoyed and deeply loved we can never lose, for all that we love deeply becomes a part of us”
items.why: Keller wrote two separate sentences; this welds them into one and changes the words along the way (“once enjoyed and deeply loved” is not her phrasing, and neither is the linking “for”). Quote Investigator ↗ finds this fused form credited to Keller in Sherokee Ilse’s Empty Arms (Wintergreen Press, 1990), page 24 — the first appearance of that wording in its citation trail — and again in a Kathy R. Floyd column in The Paris News on 4 December 1994.

Even the accurate two-sentence quote quietly drops a line. In the original the sentences are separated by: “A sunset, a mountain bathed in moonlight, the ocean in calm and in storm — we see these, love their beauty, hold the vision to our hearts.” You can read the paragraph whole in the scanned text of We Bereaved ↗.

items.who: The New Beacon Book of Quotations by Women (1996)
items.why: Quote Investigator records that Rosalie Maggio’s compilation (Beacon Press, 1996), page 411, correctly credited We Bereaved but condensed the passage significantly ↗ — a reminder that even sourced anthologies shorten as they go.

misattribution.truthLine: Keller wrote both sentences. She just did not write them side by side — the proof is on page 2 of We Bereaved, 1929 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: We Bereaved is a small book with a narrow job: 39 pages of consolation, published in New York by Leslie Fulenwider, Inc. in 1929. The passage in question sits on page 2, almost at the opening, and it lays out the whole argument the rest of the book elaborates — that what you have truly loved is not stored outside you, where it can be taken away, but inside you, where it cannot.

Coming from Helen Keller, the claim carries weight it would not carry from most writers. She had lost sight and hearing before she was two, and had spent her life arguing that a life is not diminished by what it cannot reach. Quote Investigator notes that Keller reprinted the passage in The Open Door in 1957 ↗, which carried it to a much wider readership than the 39-page 1929 original ever did.
detailsBody: Keller’s page-2 paragraph is a chain of five sentences. Quoting only the first and the third gives you the version on this page — every word Keller’s, with the sunset sentence lifted out. That is ordinary, honest condensation, and it is what most careful anthologies did.

What happened next was different. By 1990 the two sentences had been welded into one and rewritten in the process: “What we have once enjoyed and deeply loved we can never lose, for all that we love deeply becomes a part of us.” Quote Investigator finds that form in Sherokee Ilse’s Empty Arms (1990) and again in a 1994 newspaper column, both credited to Keller. It is the version that now dominates greeting cards, memorial programmes and quote sites — and it is not a sentence Keller wrote.

sourcesVerified.claim: Helen Keller's We Bereaved (1929) page 2 contains the passage beginning "What we have once enjoyed we can never lose" and including "All that we love deeply becomes a part of us"; QI concludes the popular modern statement is an altered version of Keller's words. QI's citations include We Bereaved (Leslie Fulenwider, New York, 1929, p.2), The Open Door (Doubleday, 1957, p.131), Empty Arms by Sherokee Ilse (Wintergreen Press, 1990, p.24), The Paris News 4 Dec 1994 column by Kathy R. Floyd, and The New Beacon Book of Quotations by Women (Beacon Press, 1996, p.411).

The scanned full text of We Bereaved contains the complete page-2 paragraph verbatim, including the intervening sunset sentence and the closing "Truly, life is overlord of Death and Love can never lose its own." Title page: Leslie Fulenwider, Inc., New York, 1929; copyright notice "Copyright, 1929, by Leslie Fulenwider, Inc."
The Internet Archive hosts a freely readable scan of We Bereaved by Helen Keller, Leslie Fulenwider, Inc., 1929, from the M. C. Migel Memorial Collection.
Wikimedia Commons hosts a PDF scan of Helen Keller's We Bereaved (Leslie Fulenwider, Inc., 1929), sourced from Internet Archive identifier webereaved00hele, with an explicit public-domain rationale.

Helen Keller (Helen Adams Keller), 27 June 1880 - 1 June 1968, American author, disability rights advocate, political activist and lecturer; first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree, graduating from Radcliffe College in 1904; her bibliography lists We Bereaved (1929, L. Fulenwider, Inc.).

Wikiquote's Helen Keller page does not list "What we have once enjoyed we can never lose" or "All that we love deeply becomes a part of us" in any section; it gives her dates as 27 June 1880 - 1 June 1968.
